word_order: SVO | subjects precede verbs and objects follow them in examples like 'Steve Jobs unveiled the device' and 'Mutations can have a variety of different effects'.
register: edited written informational prose (news/encyclopedic/technical), formal and non-spontaneous
fillers_and_hesitations: none in this register (no hesitation tokens in the sample)
clause_boundary_signals: subordinating conjunctions introducing dependent clauses (if, although)
relative markers/relative pronouns introducing embedded clauses (which, that)
non_boundary_traps: prepositional adjuncts that look clause-like when sentence-initial (for over, in the end)
of‑genitive noun modifiers and long noun phrases that contain internal commas (of Venezuelans, of mutation)
noun postmodifiers and participial modifiers that can mimic separate clauses (live on television, overheating)
unstable_prefix_signals: initial subordinators/clause-openers whose role is unresolved until the following clause appears (although, if)
focus/limiter words that may reverse or restrict scope once remainder appears (only, not)
notes_for_prompt_writer: This sample is edited written English with canonical SVO order and frequent use of subordinating and coordinating conjunctions. Clause boundaries are often explicitly signaled by conjunctions and relative markers, but long prepositional adjuncts and of‑phrases commonly appear at clause edges and can be mistaken for clause-ends. There are essentially no spoken hesitation tokens in this register; discourse is organized with temporal and connective phrases (e.g. 'in the end', 'once') that may precede or embed clauses.
